title: Deepgram API: Pricing, Features and Limits (2026)
summary: Deepgram API technical reference covers API key management, pricing tiers, service limits, and debugging production errors for speech-to-text deployments.
body_markdown:
## Connecting Deepgram to business tools with Activepieces


### Workflow automation and concurrency limits


Activepieces, whose core is MIT-licensed, handles the work around transcription, such as triggering on a new recording and routing the result. It doesn't do anything about your Deepgram concurrency limit, which is why it fits batch jobs and not live audio.


Your scoped Deepgram key also doesn't have to live in Activepieces' database: on a self-hosted instance or the enterprise cloud tier, connection secrets can be routed to your own secret manager, so your credentials are never ours to hold.


Point a self-hosted instance at an external secret manager and look in the database yourself, and the key isn't there; the same integration is listed beside SCIM, custom RBAC, SSO/SAML and audit logs in the enterprise feature set.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


### Making a 429 visible in a workflow


Nobody finds out until a salesperson asks why the CRM has no notes from Tuesday. That is the quiet failure this tool addresses: a call recording lands, a request goes to Deepgram, and the request comes back with a 429.


Write the glue by hand and it tends to log that error and move on.


An Activepieces flow makes you decide what happens next, because the failure is a branch you can see on the canvas, and since a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, the retry and alert branch doesn't add to the bill.


One trigger, two outcomes: that is the flow in the illustration below. A new recording starts the flow, and the flow calls Deepgram.


On success, the transcript is written to the CRM record. On failure, the flow retries, and if the retries run out, it posts an alert to a chat channel.


Outside the flow sits a separate box, labeled "live streaming: your code." Take from it that the retry and alert path covers only the left side of the picture, and that the box on the right isn't something the tool reaches.


### Why Deepgram live streaming stays in code


That boundary is deliberate. A live stream is a long-lived connection, and handling a dropped one means reconnecting, resuming from the right point in the audio and managing your own concurrency count.


A flow that runs once per event has no place to hold that state. Write that part in your own code.


### Checking for a ready-made Deepgram step


Search the community integrations directory of the open source repository, where the 750 integrations are counted and roughly 60% are community-contributed, so support quality and maintenance will vary, to see whether Deepgram has a ready-made integration step or whether you'll call it through the generic HTTP step.


The difference decides how much of the request you configure by hand, and how clearly a 429 shows up in the flow's error handling.


Whichever you use, set the retry delay with the 429 in mind: retrying immediately against a limit you've already hit only adds to the pile.
